name: KRAS
desc: ~90% of pancreatic cancers; ~40% of colorectal cancers; ~30% of lung adenocarcinomas
analogy: Cell growth signaling works like a relay race: receptor hands off to KRAS, which hands off to RAF, then MEK, then ERK. G12D lets the KRAS runner start sprinting on its own, without ever receiving the baton from the receptor.
detailedExplanation: A single base swap changes glycine to aspartate at position 12, sitting right where KRAS normally shuts itself off after passing along a growth signal. G12D blocks that shut-off step, so KRAS stays locked in its 'go' state and keeps signaling downstream continuously.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Real-time (qPCR) or digital PCR assays for G12D use a probe centered on the mutated base, detecting mutant DNA even when it's a small fraction of a tumor biopsy — used clinically to guide pancreatic and colorectal treatment choices.

name: BRAF
desc: 40-66% of melanomas; ~45-50% of papillary thyroid cancers; ~10% of colorectal
analogy: Cell growth signaling works like a relay race: receptor hands off to BRAF, which hands off to MEK, then ERK. V600E lets the BRAF runner start sprinting on its own, without ever receiving the baton from the receptor.
detailedExplanation: A single base swap changes valine to glutamate at position 600, permanently switching on the MAPK signaling pathway that tells cells to grow and divide. V600E makes up over half of all BRAF mutations and is the most common oncogenic driver in papillary thyroid carcinoma, where it's also linked to more aggressive tumor behavior.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Real-time (qPCR) assays for V600E use a fluorescent probe centered exactly on the mutated base, so signal only appears when the mutant sequence is amplified — used clinically to confirm melanoma or thyroid cancer subtype.

name: TP53
desc: Mutated in ~50-80% of all cancers; among the most common hotspots in the gene
analogy: TP53 is normally like a quality inspector at the end of a production line, halting the line whenever damaged parts (DNA errors) show up. R175H disables the inspector, so damaged cells keep moving down the line unchecked.
detailedExplanation: R175H distorts the shape of p53's DNA-binding region, so the protein can no longer attach to the genes it's meant to switch on for repair or cell-cycle arrest. The checkpoint is effectively gone even though the gene itself is still present and being expressed.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Because TP53 mutations are scattered across many hotspots rather than one dominant site, clinical testing typically sequences broader gene regions rather than using a single mutation-specific probe.

name: PIK3CA
desc: ~30-40% of hormone receptor-positive breast cancers carry this hotspot
analogy: PIK3CA acts like a dial controlling how strongly a cell responds to growth signals. H1047R snaps that dial to maximum and jams it there, so the growth response stays turned all the way up.
detailedExplanation: H1047R sits in a region of the protein that normally regulates its own activity, and the mutation removes that internal brake — the enzyme stays active and keeps converting membrane lipids into growth-promoting signals, regardless of outside cues.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — qPCR assays targeting H1047R can detect the mutation directly from tumor tissue or blood-based liquid biopsy, helping match patients to PI3K-pathway-targeted therapies.

name: EGFR
desc: ~10-15% of lung adenocarcinomas in Western patients; higher in East Asian non-smokers
analogy: EGFR sits on the cell surface like a doorbell that should only ring when a specific visitor arrives. L858R is like a doorbell stuck ringing constantly, even with nobody outside pressing it.
detailedExplanation: L858R sits in EGFR's internal kinase domain and shifts it toward the shape it normally only takes once activated from outside — so the receptor sends a continuous 'divide' signal into the cell without needing a growth factor to bind first.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Allele-specific qPCR for L858R is routinely used on lung biopsies to decide eligibility for EGFR-targeted therapies, and increasingly on blood samples to track treatment response over time.

name: MYC
desc: Amplified in a wide range of cancers; especially prominent in Burkitt lymphoma
analogy: MYC works like a master volume knob controlling hundreds of growth-related genes at once. Amplification means the cell now has extra copies of the knob itself, pushing overall volume far above normal.
detailedExplanation: Rather than one broken letter, amplification means the cell carries extra copies of the entire MYC gene, producing far more MYC protein than usual. Because MYC controls the activity of a huge number of downstream genes, this excess drives proliferation broadly rather than through one single pathway step.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Copy-number is typically measured with quantitative PCR comparing MYC gene dosage against a reference gene, rather than a mutation-specific probe, since there's no single altered base to target.

name: PTEN
desc: Lost in a large share of endometrial cancers and glioblastomas
analogy: PTEN acts like the brake pedal opposing PI3K's accelerator. R130G is like cutting that brake line — the accelerator stays effectively unopposed, even without being pressed any harder than usual.
detailedExplanation: PTEN normally reverses the chemical mark that PI3K adds to membrane lipids, directly counteracting PI3K's growth signal. R130G disrupts this enzymatic activity, so the mark isn't erased and growth signaling stays elevated by default.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Because PTEN loss can occur via many different mutations or deletions, testing often screens the whole gene region rather than one specific hotspot probe.

name: RB1
desc: Near-universal loss in retinoblastoma; also lost in many small-cell lung cancers
analogy: RB1 works like a gatekeeper holding a door shut until the cell is genuinely ready to divide. A deletion removes the gatekeeper entirely, so the door swings open on its own.
detailedExplanation: RB1 encodes a protein that binds and restrains other proteins needed to enter the cell-division cycle. When RB1 is deleted, that restraint is simply absent — there's no protein left to hold the checkpoint closed, so cells enter division more freely.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Deletions are typically detected via copy-number PCR (checking whether the RB1 region is present at all) rather than a sequence-specific mutation probe.

name: APC
desc: Mutated in the majority of colorectal cancers, often as an early event
analogy: APC normally works like a shredder that destroys a growth-signal protein (beta-catenin) as fast as it accumulates. This mutation is like breaking the shredder partway through assembly — it stops working, so the growth-signal protein piles up.
detailedExplanation: The asterisk in R1450* marks a premature stop signal in the DNA, so the protein is cut short partway through. APC's job is to mark beta-catenin for destruction; a truncated APC can't do this, so beta-catenin accumulates and switches on growth genes it normally wouldn't reach.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Premature stop mutations like this can be detected with allele-specific PCR, and are also a class of interest for experimental base-editing correction approaches.

name: BRCA1
desc: Inherited mutations sharply raise lifetime breast and ovarian cancer risk
analogy: BRCA1 is like a repair crew that fixes breaks in DNA's double strand cleanly. This mutation deletes two letters early in the gene's instructions, scrambling everything written after — like a typo early in a sentence that turns the rest into gibberish.
detailedExplanation: 185delAG is a frameshift mutation: deleting 2 base pairs shifts how the rest of the code is read in groups of three, garbling the downstream protein sequence and typically triggering an early stop. The resulting BRCA1 protein can't repair double-strand DNA breaks properly, so errors accumulate over time.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Allele-specific PCR for 185delAG is used in genetic testing (notably common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations) to identify carriers before cancer develops, enabling earlier screening.

name: HER2 (ERBB2)
desc: Amplified in roughly 15-20% of breast cancers; defines a distinct treatment subtype
analogy: HER2 is a growth-signal receptor on the cell surface, like a receiving antenna. Amplification means the cell builds far more antennas than usual, picking up and relaying growth signals much more strongly.
detailedExplanation: Like MYC, this is a copy-number change rather than a point mutation — the cell carries extra copies of the HER2 gene, producing more receptor protein on its surface. More receptors means more simultaneous growth-signal relay, driving faster proliferation.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — HER2 amplification is measured via quantitative PCR or FISH comparing HER2 gene copy number to a reference, directly guiding eligibility for HER2-targeted antibody therapy.

name: BCL2
desc: Present in ~85-90% of follicular lymphomas via a chromosomal translocation
analogy: BCL2 normally acts like a lock holding the cell's self-destruct trigger in place until it's genuinely needed. The t(14;18) translocation moves BCL2 next to a hyperactive promoter, so the cell manufactures far more of that lock than it should — jamming the self-destruct mechanism shut.
detailedExplanation: The translocation fuses the BCL2 gene to a strong antibody-gene promoter (IGH), driving massive overproduction of BCL2 protein. BCL2 sits on the mitochondrial membrane and binds the pro-apoptotic proteins (like BAX) that would normally trigger cell death — with BCL2 flooding the cell, that death signal never gets through, so damaged B cells that should die keep surviving and accumulating.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Because the t(14;18) breakpoint is unique to where the chromosomes fused, PCR primers spanning that specific junction are used both to diagnose the translocation and to monitor for minimal residual disease after treatment.

name: BRCA2
desc: Inherited mutations raise lifetime breast, ovarian, and pancreatic cancer risk
analogy: BRCA2 works alongside BRCA1 on the same repair crew, but handles a different part of the job — guiding the actual repair machinery to the break site. 6174delT deletes a single letter, shifting the reading frame so the rest of the repair-crew instructions come out scrambled.
detailedExplanation: 6174delT is a single base-pair deletion causing a frameshift, similar in effect to BRCA1's 185delAG. It disrupts BRCA2's role in loading the RAD51 protein onto damaged DNA, a key step in accurately repairing double-strand breaks. Without functional BRCA2, cells rely on sloppier backup repair pathways, letting errors accumulate.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Like other founder mutations, 6174delT is tested for with allele-specific PCR, commonly as part of hereditary cancer panels alongside BRCA1.

name: CCND1
desc: Amplified in roughly 15-20% of breast cancers; also driven by translocation in mantle cell lymphoma
analogy: CCND1 encodes cyclin D1, which works like a green light telling the cell it's clear to start dividing. Amplification means far more green lights are installed than normal, so the 'go' signal is essentially always lit.
detailedExplanation: Cyclin D1 partners with cell-cycle kinases to push the cell past its first major checkpoint into active division. Extra CCND1 copies mean the checkpoint is passed more easily and more often, even when the cell hasn't received the growth signals that would normally justify it.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Copy-number is assessed with quantitative PCR or FISH; in mantle cell lymphoma, a t(11;14) translocation breakpoint PCR is used instead, since the mechanism there is a rearrangement rather than amplification.

name: ALK
desc: Found in roughly 3-5% of non-small cell lung cancers, usually in younger, light or never-smokers
analogy: A gene fusion is like two different instruction manuals getting bound together into one. Here, the EML4 gene's 'always on' front section gets stitched onto ALK's growth-signaling back section, so ALK signals constantly instead of only when properly triggered.
detailedExplanation: A chromosomal rearrangement fuses part of the EML4 gene to the ALK gene, creating a novel fusion protein. The EML4 portion causes the fused protein to clump together on its own, which is normally what happens only after ALK is activated — so the fusion protein sends continuous growth signals without needing any outside trigger.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Break-apart FISH or RT-PCR spanning the fusion junction is used clinically to detect EML4-ALK, directly determining eligibility for ALK-inhibitor therapy in lung cancer.

name: ROS1
desc: Found in roughly 1-2% of non-small cell lung cancers
analogy: Similar to the ALK fusion, ROS1 gets stitched to a partner gene (often CD74) whose piece forces the fused protein to activate itself constantly, bypassing the normal 'wait for a signal' step entirely.
detailedExplanation: ROS1 is a receptor-type kinase that normally needs an external signal to activate. The fusion partner supplies a segment that causes constant self-clustering of the fusion protein, mimicking permanent activation and driving continuous downstream growth signaling.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — RT-PCR or break-apart FISH targeting the fusion junction identifies ROS1-rearranged tumors, which respond to a specific class of targeted inhibitors distinct from EGFR or ALK drugs.

name: STK11 (LKB1)
desc: Mutated in roughly 15-20% of lung adenocarcinomas, often alongside KRAS
analogy: STK11 acts like an energy monitor that pumps the brakes on cell growth whenever resources run low. Loss-of-function mutations disconnect the monitor entirely, so the cell keeps growing even under conditions where it normally should pause.
detailedExplanation: STK11 activates a downstream sensor (AMPK) that halts growth and division when a cell's energy or nutrient supply is stressed. When STK11 is lost, this brake disappears, letting cells keep proliferating under conditions that would normally trigger a slowdown — and tumors with STK11 loss also tend to respond less well to immunotherapy.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Because STK11 loss can happen through many different mutation types or deletions across the gene, testing typically sequences broader regions rather than targeting one specific hotspot.

name: MET
desc: Found in roughly 3-4% of lung adenocarcinomas, more common in older patients
analogy: MET is normally tagged for breakdown after it finishes sending a growth signal, the way a used ticket gets punched so it can't be reused. Exon 14 skipping removes the part of the instructions coding for that 'punch' tag, so the receptor keeps getting recycled and reused instead of destroyed.
detailedExplanation: A splicing error causes the cell to skip exon 14 entirely when building the MET protein, removing the docking site normally used to mark the receptor for degradation after signaling. Without that tag, MET protein accumulates at the cell surface and keeps signaling far longer than it should.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — RT-PCR designed across the exon 13-15 junction detects the abnormal splicing directly, which is the standard way MET exon 14 skipping is confirmed clinically.

name: CDH1
desc: Inherited mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer syndrome
analogy: CDH1 encodes E-cadherin, which works like the glue holding neighboring cells together in a sheet. A truncating mutation breaks that glue, letting individual cells detach and drift away from the tissue they belong to.
detailedExplanation: E-cadherin sits on the cell surface and physically links neighboring cells together, keeping tissue organized. A truncating mutation produces a shortened, non-functional protein, so cells lose their grip on each other. This is thought to explain why CDH1-related gastric cancer grows diffusely through the stomach wall rather than as one solid mass.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Because mutations are scattered across the gene, hereditary diffuse gastric cancer testing sequences the full CDH1 gene rather than checking one hotspot.

name: SMAD4
desc: Lost in roughly half of pancreatic cancers, often at a more advanced stage
analogy: SMAD4 relays a 'stop growing' message from outside the cell to the nucleus, like a messenger carrying an order to halt. Deletion removes the messenger, so the stop order never arrives even when the outside signal is still being sent.
detailedExplanation: SMAD4 sits downstream of TGF-beta signaling, a pathway that normally restrains cell division. When SMAD4 is deleted, the cell can no longer relay that restraining signal into the nucleus, so TGF-beta's growth-suppressing effect is lost even though the outside signal itself is intact.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Deletions are typically identified with copy-number PCR, checking whether the SMAD4 region is present, rather than a single sequence-specific probe.

name: MLH1
desc: Inherited mutations cause Lynch syndrome, sharply raising colorectal and endometrial cancer risk
analogy: MLH1 works like a proofreader checking freshly copied DNA for typos before the cell moves on. A loss-of-function mutation removes the proofreader, so small copying errors slip through uncorrected every time the cell divides.
detailedExplanation: MLH1 is part of the mismatch repair system that corrects errors made when DNA is copied. Without functional MLH1, these small errors accumulate rapidly across many genes with each cell division, a pattern known as microsatellite instability — dramatically raising the odds that a critical growth-control gene eventually gets knocked out too.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Microsatellite instability testing uses PCR to compare short repeat sequences in tumor versus normal tissue, flagging mismatch-repair failure indirectly rather than testing MLH1 itself.

name: BCR-ABL1
desc: Defines chronic myeloid leukemia; present in nearly all cases
analogy: A piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 swap places and fuse, creating a new hybrid gene, BCR-ABL1, like two different machines welded into one that never stops running once switched on.
detailedExplanation: The fusion joins BCR to the ABL1 kinase gene, and the BCR portion forces the resulting protein to constantly activate itself without needing any outside signal. This drives continuous, unregulated production of white blood cells — the defining feature of chronic myeloid leukemia.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — RT-PCR across the BCR-ABL1 fusion junction is the standard test both for diagnosis and for monitoring how well a patient is responding to treatment over time.

name: FLT3
desc: Found in roughly 25-30% of acute myeloid leukemia cases
analogy: An internal tandem duplication is like accidentally photocopying a paragraph twice into the same document. The extra repeated segment jams the receptor into an active shape, so it signals nonstop instead of only when triggered.
detailedExplanation: A stretch of DNA within the FLT3 gene gets duplicated and reinserted, lengthening part of the receptor. This structural change locks the receptor into an active conformation, driving continuous downstream signaling that pushes myeloid cells to divide uncontrollably. ITD-positive AML is also generally associated with a higher relapse risk.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Fragment-length PCR is used to detect the duplicated segment directly, since the mutation changes the size of the amplified DNA fragment rather than just a single base.

name: NPM1
desc: Found in roughly 30% of acute myeloid leukemia cases, often with a relatively favorable prognosis
analogy: NPM1 normally shuttles proteins in and out of the nucleus, like a courier with an ID badge that only lets it operate inside the building. This mutation adds extra letters that create a new 'exit only' tag, forcing the protein out into the wrong part of the cell where it behaves abnormally.
detailedExplanation: A small insertion in exon 12 shifts NPM1's reading frame, creating a new signal that relocates the protein from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. This mislocalization disrupts NPM1's normal tumor-suppressive interactions in the nucleus, contributing to leukemic transformation even though the mutation itself doesn't touch a growth-signaling pathway directly.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Fragment-length PCR detects the small insertion by the shift it causes in amplified fragment size, and is also used to track minimal residual disease during treatment.

name: JAK2
desc: Found in the large majority of polycythemia vera cases and roughly half of the other myeloproliferative disorders
analogy: JAK2 normally only switches on after a growth-factor receptor tells it to. V617F is like a switch with a jammed spring — it flips to 'on' and stays there, sending signals whether or not the receptor ever gets its expected input.
detailedExplanation: A single base swap changes valine to phenylalanine at position 617, disrupting a region that normally keeps the JAK2 kinase inactive until instructed. With that self-inhibition broken, JAK2 signals continuously, driving bone marrow to overproduce blood cells independent of the hormones that would normally control that process.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Allele-specific qPCR for V617F is a standard diagnostic test for myeloproliferative disorders, and can also estimate what fraction of blood cells carry the mutation.

name: MYD88
desc: Found in over 90% of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia cases
analogy: MYD88 normally only relays a signal after an immune alarm (like a detected infection) sets it off. L265P is like an alarm relay stuck permanently triggered, continuously telling downstream immune-cell growth pathways to activate even with no real threat present.
detailedExplanation: A single base swap changes leucine to proline at position 265, causing MYD88 to spontaneously self-associate and activate downstream signaling without needing to be triggered by an actual immune receptor. This constant activation drives survival and proliferation signals in B cells, contributing to lymphoma development.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Allele-specific PCR for L265P is used clinically to help distinguish Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia from other similar-looking blood disorders.

name: NRAS
desc: Found in roughly 15-20% of melanomas, often mutually exclusive with BRAF mutations
analogy: Like KRAS, NRAS acts as an on/off switch that's supposed to reset itself after each growth signal. Q61R jams that reset mechanism, so once flipped on, the switch stays stuck in the 'go' position.
detailedExplanation: A single base swap changes glutamine to arginine at position 61, interfering with NRAS's own built-in shut-off mechanism. Normally the protein deactivates itself shortly after relaying a growth signal; this mutation blocks that step, keeping downstream growth signaling continuously active.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Allele-specific qPCR targeting Q61R helps distinguish NRAS-driven melanomas from BRAF-driven ones, which respond to different classes of targeted therapy.

name: CDKN2A
desc: Inherited mutations are the most common cause of familial melanoma
analogy: CDKN2A encodes a protein (p16) that works like a wheel clamp on the cell-cycle machinery, physically preventing it from rolling forward. Deletion removes the clamp entirely, letting the machinery roll ahead unchecked.
detailedExplanation: p16 normally blocks the kinases that push a cell past its main growth checkpoint, acting as a direct brake on cell-cycle progression. When CDKN2A is deleted, that brake is gone, so cells move through the checkpoint far more easily — one reason inherited CDKN2A loss carries such a strong familial melanoma risk.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Deletions are identified through copy-number PCR, checking whether the CDKN2A region is present, since the loss often spans the whole gene rather than a single point mutation.

name: EWSR1-FLI1
desc: Present in roughly 85% of Ewing sarcoma cases; defines the disease
analogy: This fusion is like swapping the plug on one appliance for the plug of a much more powerful power source — the FLI1 gene, which normally controls cell identity genes, gets wired to EWSR1's high-output activation piece, forcing those genes on far beyond normal levels.
detailedExplanation: A translocation joins part of the EWSR1 gene to the FLI1 gene, creating a fusion protein where EWSR1's strong activation domain drives FLI1's gene-targeting domain. The result switches on a set of genes that push bone and soft-tissue precursor cells toward aggressive, undifferentiated growth rather than normal development.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — RT-PCR spanning the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion junction is the standard confirmatory test, since Ewing sarcoma can otherwise resemble other small round-cell tumors under a microscope.

name: MDM2
desc: Amplified in the large majority of well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas
analogy: MDM2 normally acts like a disposal service for p53, keeping its levels in check under everyday conditions. Amplification means the cell hires far too many disposal crews, so p53 gets cleared out and destroyed even when it's badly needed to respond to damage.
detailedExplanation: MDM2 tags the p53 protein for degradation, keeping p53 levels low during normal conditions. When MDM2 is amplified, the cell produces excess MDM2 protein that continuously clears out p53 — effectively disabling the p53 checkpoint without ever mutating TP53 itself.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — MDM2 amplification is confirmed with quantitative PCR or FISH comparing gene copy number to a reference, a key diagnostic step for distinguishing liposarcoma from benign fatty tumors.

name: WT1
desc: Mutated in roughly 10-15% of Wilms tumors, a childhood kidney cancer
analogy: WT1 works like a foreman overseeing kidney tissue as it matures properly during development. A loss-of-function mutation removes the foreman, so precursor kidney cells never receive the instructions to stop dividing and mature normally.
detailedExplanation: WT1 is a transcription factor essential for normal kidney and gonadal development, switching on genes that guide precursor cells toward mature, non-dividing kidney tissue. When WT1 is lost, those precursor cells fail to mature and instead keep dividing, forming the immature-looking tumor tissue characteristic of Wilms tumor.
crisprTargeting: PCR strategy — Because WT1 mutations are scattered across the gene, hereditary and tumor testing typically sequences broader gene regions rather than checking a single hotspot.
